# Guiding the Ward and Ministering to the Family

## First principles

- **Her membership status is not ward business.** Resignation (or any membership action) is between her, the bishop, and the Lord. It is not announced, debated, or adjudicated in elders quorum, Relief Society, or the foyer. Full stop.
- **The pulpit is not a press release.** The ward does not "publicly side" with anyone — not with her, not against her. Sacrament meeting is for Christ, not for taking positions on a sister's Facebook post.
- **Doctrine doesn't change because feelings are tender, and love doesn't shrink because doctrine is firm.** Both are true at once. A bishopric that forgets either one will fail this family.

## To members demanding she be "called to repentance"

I'd say something like this, privately and gently:

> "Thank you for caring about her soul. That impulse is good. But calling someone to repentance is the stewardship of the Lord, her bishop, and her own conscience — not ours. Our stewardship right now is to love her, to love her son, and to make sure neither of them ever hears that the Church chewed them over in a hallway. If you feel prompted to reach out, reach out with bread, not a sermon."

I would not entertain efforts to organize a response, a letter, or a "concerned members" conversation. That's contention dressed up as righteousness.

## To members demanding the ward publicly side with her

Similarly, privately:

> "I understand. Many of us ache for families in this situation, and her love for her son is the kind of love we hope every parent has. But the ward as an institution doesn't issue statements on members' personal decisions — for her protection as much as anyone's. What we *can* do is be the kind of ward where her son would feel safe walking through the door. That's louder than any statement."

## Ministering to her and her family

- **Call her.** Not to discuss her decision, not to negotiate, not to "work on her." Just to say: *We love you. You are not erased from our hearts. The door is open whenever, for whatever — a meal, a hug, a hard conversation, nothing at all.*
- **Keep ministering assignments active** unless and until she asks otherwise. Resignation removes her name from a record; it does not remove her from the body of Christ in our eyes.
- **Reach out to the son directly, if appropriate** — through her, with her blessing. A short, sincere note from the bishop: *You are loved. You are welcome here anytime. I'm sorry for any pain our community has caused you.* No agenda. No invitation to a meeting. Just the truth.
- **The husband and any other children** are also in grief and in a hard spot socially. Make sure their home teachers/ministering brothers and sisters are present and unweird.

## Teaching the ward going forward

Without ever naming her, I would, over coming weeks, teach plainly from the pulpit and in council:

- The Savior's pattern: truth and grace, never one without the other.
- That our doctrine on marriage is what the prophets have taught — and that our doctrine on the worth of souls, including our LGBTQ brothers and sisters and their families, is also what the prophets have taught (see President Nelson, President Oaks, *Saints* vol. 4 framing, and the Church's own "Love One Another" materials).
- That gossip about another member's standing is itself a sin worth repenting of.
- That a ward is measured by whether the hurting feel safe in it.

## What I would *not* do

- Discuss her case in ward council beyond "her family needs ministering — who has the relationship?"
- Allow any lesson, talk, or comment that uses her as an example, positive or negative.
- Pretend nothing happened. Silence reads as judgment. Quiet, specific love does not.
- Make her son a project. He is a person.

## The bishopric's own posture

We kneel. We counsel together. We remember that we will answer for how we treated this mother and this young man — not for whether we successfully defended an institution that does not need our defending. The Church can hold its own doctrine. Our job is to hold the people.

> *"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another."* — John 13:35

That's the assignment. Everything else is noise.

**First, what I would not do.**

I would not counsel anyone to "call her to repentance," and I would not convene a membership council. Withdrawal of membership on request is an administrative matter, not a disciplinary one. When a member asks to have her name removed, my role — following the General Handbook — is to confirm that the request is her own, informed, and voluntary, and then forward it through the stake president. It is not an occasion for an interview designed to talk her out of it, and there is no basis for discipline in a person exercising her right to leave. I would say that plainly to anyone who raises it, and then I would say the second thing: her membership status and any conversation I have with her are confidential. I will not discuss them over the pulpit or in a hallway, and I will not confirm, deny, or correct details of what she posted.

I also would not have the ward issue a public statement siding with her. A bishopric does not speak publicly for the Church; official positions come from the First Presidency. More to the point, a ward is not a party to a social-media argument, and taking a public side would convert this family's private grief into the ward's content. That is a boundary, not a dodge, and I would explain it in those terms to the members who want it.

**Ministering to her.**

I would contact her personally and privately, and soon — a phone call or a visit at her convenience, not a delegated assignment. The purpose is not retention. I would thank her for what she has given this ward, tell her I love her, tell her I am sorry her son felt unwelcome here, and ask nothing of her. She is welcome in the building, at the ward Christmas party, at her grandchild's baptism, and in my home. I would say explicitly that no one is going to be assigned to work on her and that she will not be the subject of a reactivation campaign. Welcome that is contingent on her changing her mind is not welcome; it is leverage, and she would recognize it instantly.

**Ministering to her son.**

This is the part that matters most and the part most easily fumbled. His claim is that he felt unwelcome. The response to that claim is not an argument that he was mistaken. It is actual welcome. If he is willing to talk with me, I would ask him — genuinely, without a rebuttal loaded behind my teeth — what being welcome here would have looked like, and what it would look like now, and then I would fix what I can fix. I would keep in mind that LGBTQ members and youth in religious communities carry real and elevated risk of despair and self-harm, and that "he is not on our records" does not release me from a duty of care toward someone in this ward's orbit.

**Protecting the rest of the family.**

Other family members are likely still attending, and they will be watched, pitied, and asked about it. I would meet with them, ask what they want said and not said, and instruct the Relief Society and elders quorum presidencies and their ministering brothers and sisters concretely — not only what to do (invite, include, be normal with them) but what not to say: no probing, no "we're praying for your mother," no theories about who is to blame. Ordinary friendship, offered consistently, is the whole assignment.

**Teaching the ward.**

I would not address the post from the pulpit as an event; that would only amplify it. I would redirect gossip privately, in the moment, each time it surfaces — "I'm not going to talk about her, and I'd ask you not to either." Over the following months I would have us teach principles rather than the incident: the two great commandments, charity as the pure love of Christ, President Nelson's call for peacemakers, and President Oaks's teaching on loving others while living with differences.

And I would hold two things together without hedging either one. The doctrine of marriage between a man and a woman is not being renegotiated by me, and I will not pretend otherwise to make anyone comfortable. At the same time, experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin, our doors are open, and our love for a person is not contingent on his or her agreement with us. The Church itself moved in 2019 to reverse the 2015 policy regarding children of parents in same-sex relationships — evidence that "you are unwelcome" was never the intended message, however often it has been the received one.

**How I would measure whether I did this right.**

Not by whether she comes back. By whether, a year from now, she would still take my call; whether her son believes he could walk into our building without bracing; whether her family is still surrounded by friends rather than by observers; and whether the members who wanted a fight found, in me, nothing to fight with.

# Guiding the Ward and Ministering to This Family

This situation has several layers — a public resignation, a polarized ward, a mother's pain, and a son who felt unwelcome. Each requires a distinct pastoral response.

---

## 1. Immediately: Quiet the Polarization

Both factions — those wanting public repentance and those wanting the ward to "side with her" — are treating a family's pain as a cause to rally around. Gently redirect in both cases:

- **To those demanding she be "called to repentance":** Membership resignation is a personal, protected decision processed through Church headquarters. It is not the ward's role to publicly adjudicate it. Remind them that the Savior's model was never to shame people back into the fold. "If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue… this man's religion is vain" (James 1:26). Ask them: *What do you think the Savior would do right now — organize a correction, or go sit with her?*

- **To those wanting the ward to publicly "side with her":** The ward cannot issue a public statement contradicting Church doctrine, and doing so would simply create a new wound. But validate their instinct: their desire to stand with a hurting person is Christlike. Channel it into personal, private ministry rather than public declarations.

- **In ward council:** Ask leaders to refrain from discussing her situation on social media entirely, and to discourage others from doing so. This family's story is not content. It's a sacred trust.

---

## 2. Personally: Go to Her

Don't wait. Don't send a text. You or the bishop go to her home — not to discuss her membership status, not to persuade her to return, but simply to say:

> *"We love you. We love your son. Your family matters to us regardless of what any membership record says. We are here. How are you doing?"*

Then **listen**. Her announcement likely came after months or years of anguish. She didn't wake up one day and decide this. She watched her son suffer and concluded she had to choose. Whether that conclusion is doctrinally accurate is far less important right now than the fact that **a mother is in pain and she felt the Church was the source of it.**

Do not, in this visit, attempt to correct her framing. Ministry precedes teaching. Always.

---

## 3. Honestly: Examine the Ward's Role

Her son "felt unwelcome." That deserves serious reflection, not defensiveness. In ward council, ask plainly:

- Do our lessons and talks discuss same-sex attraction with compassion, or only as a cautionary abstraction?
- Would an LGBTQ member or visitor hear anything from our pulpit or in our hallways that tells them God loves them and there is a place for them here?
- Have we created a culture where people with complicated questions feel safe, or one where they learn to stay silent?

This is not about changing doctrine. The Church's position on the law of chastity and the nature of marriage is what it is. But **doctrine and culture are not the same thing**, and wards are responsible for the culture they build. Elder Christofferson has been clear that having same-sex attraction is not a sin, and the Church's own materials emphasize belonging. If the ward culture didn't reflect that, own it.

---

## 4. Practically: Minister to the Whole Family

- **Assign or keep ministering brothers and sisters** for the family, choosing people with high emotional intelligence who won't treat visits as reconversion projects. The assignment: *love them, period.*
- **The son** — if he's still in the area, make sure he knows he is welcome at any activity, any service project, any dinner. Welcome is not contingent on belief or conformity. A young man who felt rejected by his faith community carries a wound the ward has some responsibility to help heal, not deepen.
- **The father and any siblings** — they are navigating this too. Don't let them become invisible in the drama.

---

## 5. Doctrinally: Hold the Tension Honestly

Some ward members will press: *"But aren't we supposed to stand for truth?"* Yes. And here is the truth:

- The doctrine of marriage as between a man and a woman is the Church's position and it has not changed.
- The doctrine of the worth of souls is equally binding. "Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God" (D&C 18:10) has no asterisk.
- The second great commandment is not a suggestion, and Jesus did not add "except when it's complicated."
- People are allowed to leave. Agency — the right to choose, even in ways we grieve — is not a failure of the plan. It *is* the plan.

The bishopric's role is not to resolve the tension between these truths by collapsing one into the other. It is to **hold both fully** and to lead a ward that can do the same — a ward where doctrine is clear *and* every person who walks through the door (or chooses not to) is treated as someone the Savior would seek out.

---

## Summary of Practical Steps

| Action | Owner | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Visit the family personally, listen | Bishop or counselor | This week |
| Ward council discussion: redirect polarization, examine ward culture | Bishopric | Next ward council |
| Assign/brief compassionate ministering siblings/brothers | Elders/RS presidencies | This week |
| Privately ask ward members to stay off social media on this topic | Bishopric, informally | Immediately |
| Reach out to the son specifically | Someone he trusts, with bishop's awareness | Soon, naturally |
| Teach the ward over time (not reactively) about Christlike inclusion | Bishopric via talks, lessons | Coming months |

---

The measure of a ward is not whether everyone stays. It's whether everyone — those who stay, those who leave, and those who aren't sure — can say: *"They loved me."*

## Pastoral Guidance: Navigating a Public Resignation Over LGBTQ Issues

### I. Clarify What Is Not Your Role

Before acting, establish what a bishopric should *not* do here:

- **Do not publicly adjudicate her decision.** Her resignation is between her and the Lord. A bishop does not issue public verdicts on members' choices.
- **Do not take institutional "sides."** The ward is not a constituency to be mobilized. Both camps urging you toward a public posture are asking you to do something a shepherd shouldn't do.
- **Do not let the ward fracture.** The loudest voices rarely represent the whole; your job is to hold the community together while being honest about doctrine.

---

### II. Address the Ward's Divided Reactions (Privately, Not From the Pulpit)

**To those wanting her "called to repentance":**
Counsel them privately and gently. This impulse, however sincere, confuses discipline with discipleship. She has not been charged with any formal matter; she has made a painful personal decision. The Savior's pattern was to pursue the one who left — not to pronounce judgment from a distance. Invite these members to ask themselves: *What would cause her to want to return? Is this posture the answer?*

**To those wanting the ward to publicly endorse her position:**
Counsel them privately as well. The Church's doctrinal position on marriage is not something a ward council can override, and performing a public endorsement would be dishonest to the members who hold that doctrine sincerely. Solidarity expressed as doctrinal capitulation is not real solidarity.

**To the ward generally:**
Do not address this from the pulpit unless it has already become a ward-wide disruption. If you must speak to it broadly, model the tone: *"We love Sister [Name] and her family. How we treat people who disagree with us or leave is a measure of our discipleship. Let's make sure she knows she's still loved here."*

---

### III. Distinguish the Real Issues

There are at least *three distinct things* that have been conflated in her announcement:

| Issue | Church's Position | Pastoral Posture |
|---|---|---|
| Doctrine on same-sex marriage | Clear, unchanged | Acknowledge honestly; don't soften or weaponize |
| How her son was treated by ward members | Separate from doctrine; possibly genuinely hurtful | Own it where warranted; this may be legitimate grievance |
| Her decision to resign | Her agency; cannot be undone by argument | Respect it while keeping the door open |

The key pastoral insight: **her son may have experienced real unkindness, not merely disagreement with doctrine.** Those are different. The Church teaches that LGBTQ individuals are children of God deserving dignity and welcome as people. If ward members treated him otherwise, that is a failure worth acknowledging — without abandoning doctrine.

---

### IV. Minister to Her and Her Son Directly

**Visit her — not to argue, not to "fix," not to recruit her back.** Visit because she is still in your stewardship spiritually, still your neighbor, still beloved. Objectives for that visit:

1. Express genuine love without an agenda.
2. Listen to her grief as a mother. Her pain is real. Honor it.
3. Do not make the visit about her resignation or her doctrinal disagreement. That is not why you're there.
4. Let her know the ward's door is open to her and to her son — *as people*, not as a project.

**Regarding her son:** If there is access and appropriateness, ensure he knows that the ward sees him as a person of worth. His feeling unwelcome may reflect real failures by ward members (not just disagreement with policy). A bishop who acknowledges *"I'm sorry you felt unwelcome here — you matter to us"* is not abandoning doctrine. He is practicing it.

---

### V. The Long Game

Her resignation is an ending of one kind of membership, not of relationship. Some people come back; many don't for years; some never do. Your job is not to engineer a particular outcome but to ensure:

- The ward remains a place her son *could* walk into and be treated with dignity.
- She knows she is loved without conditions attached to that love.
- The ward learns, through your example, that love and doctrinal fidelity are not in competition.
- The members who are watching how you handle this see that the Church responds to pain with pastoral care, not political positioning.

---

### Summary Principle

> *Maintain doctrine with clarity. Minister to persons with charity. Refuse to let the ward be conscripted into either vindication or condemnation. The shepherd's job is to keep the door open and the light on.*

# Navigating Family, Faith, and a Daughter's Same-Sex Marriage

## Start from the doctrine the Church has actually taught about *family*

Latter-day Saint doctrine on the nature of marriage hasn't changed: the Proclamation on the Family still teaches that marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God. But that same doctrine is bracketed by an equally clear teaching — that families are the unit through which God's love is meant to flow, and that "the worth of souls is great in the sight of God" (D&C 18:10). A faithful family does not have to choose between holding the doctrine and holding their daughter. The Church's own published guidance, and the public counsel of apostles like Elder D. Todd Christofferson (whose brother is in a same-sex relationship) and Elder Dale G. Renlund, is explicit: keep them close.

## Concrete principles for the family

1. **Keep her at the table — literally.** Sunday dinner, holidays, birthdays, grandkids' baptisms, school plays. Withdrawing invitations is not a defense of doctrine; it is a withdrawal of covenant love. President Nelson has taught that the gathering of Israel begins in our own homes. You cannot gather someone you have pushed out the door.

2. **Welcome her wife as you would any in-law.** Use her name. Ask about her work. Remember her birthday. Treating her with ordinary courtesy and warmth is not a doctrinal statement about the marriage; it is a doctrinal statement about her as a child of Heavenly Parents. Coldness toward her will be read — correctly — as coldness toward your daughter and grandchildren.

3. **Love the grandchildren without conditions or asterisks.** Since 2019 the Church has made clear that children of same-sex couples may be blessed, baptized, and fully participate. Grandparents have an enormous role to play; don't forfeit it.

4. **Distinguish *welcoming* from *endorsing*.** Christ ate with publicans and sinners without ever ratifying their choices, and no one accused Him of "normalizing sin" — except the people He was rebuking. A family can love, host, and include without delivering speeches of approval. Silence about a relationship at the dinner table is not endorsement; it is hospitality.

5. **Let parents teach their own children.** The cousins are not catechized by the seating chart at Thanksgiving; they are catechized by their own parents in family scripture study and family home evening. If relatives are worried about "confusion," the answer is for *those* parents to teach their *own* children plainly and lovingly about the Church's doctrine of marriage, the reality that good people we love sometimes live differently than the gospel teaches, and that we love them anyway. That is a more faithful lesson than exclusion would ever be.

6. **Don't make her relationship the topic every time you see her.** She knows what you believe. She knows what the temple recommend questions ask. Constant re-litigation is not ministering; it is nagging, and it ends relationships. Save doctrinal conversations for when she invites them, and have them with humility.

7. **Be honest about your own limits without weaponizing them.** It is fine to say, "I love you, I want you here, and I also still believe what the Church teaches about marriage — I'm not going to pretend otherwise, and I trust you not to expect me to." That is more honest, and more sustainable, than either pretending you've changed your mind or pretending she doesn't exist.

## How to answer the relatives who object

- **"It normalizes sin."** The Savior's pattern was proximity, not distance. Excluding family does not protect doctrine; it just produces estrangement and, often, the loss of any spiritual influence at all. Many parents who chose exclusion have publicly grieved that choice; very few who chose love have.
- **"It confuses the cousins."** Children are not confused by being told the truth. They *are* confused — and wounded — by watching adults they love be treated as unpersons. Teach the doctrine in your home; show the love at the gathering. Both are possible.
- **"What about my agency to set a boundary?"** A boundary protects you from harm; it does not punish someone for existing. Refusing to attend a sealing your daughter cannot have is one thing. Refusing to let her into your kitchen is another.

## The underlying counsel

President Russell M. Nelson has repeatedly taught that the Lord loves *every* one of His children and asked Latter-day Saints to do the same. Elder Christofferson, speaking about his own family, has said the relationship with his brother is "one of love." Elder Jeffrey R. Holland has pleaded for parents not to give up on any child. The faithful path is not the path of distance. It is the harder, slower, more Christlike path of staying — holding the doctrine quietly and the daughter tightly, week after week, dinner after dinner, until the Lord sorts the rest of it out in His own time and His own way.

Keep her coming. Keep her wife welcome. Keep the grandkids close. That *is* the faithful answer.

## The short answer

Latter‑day Saint teaching does not require a family to choose between doctrinal fidelity and keeping a daughter. It asks for both: hold the doctrine of marriage without amendment, and hold the relationship without conditions. Inclusion at a dinner table is not doctrinal endorsement, and the Church has never taught that it is.

## What the doctrine actually says — and doesn't

- **The teaching stands.** *The Family: A Proclamation to the World* defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and the law of chastity confines sexual relations to that marriage. A civil same-sex marriage is contrary to that standard, and no family gathering changes it. Nobody has to pretend otherwise.
- **The 2015 handbook policy was rescinded in April 2019.** Entering a same-sex marriage is treated as a serious transgression, but it is no longer labeled apostasy, membership councils are not mandatory, and **children of such couples may receive blessings and baptism without special approval.** Families still operating on the 2015 framing are working from a policy the First Presidency itself reversed.
- **The Handbook's pastoral direction is explicit** (§38.6.15 and related): members and leaders are to reach out with love, kindness, and civility, and are told that unkind treatment of LGBTQ individuals is not consistent with the Savior's teachings.
- **Church leaders have addressed this exact scenario.** Elder D. Todd Christofferson, asked in 2015 whether a gay child in a relationship could still be welcomed home, answered essentially yes — this is still your child, still welcome in your home. Elder Quentin L. Cook has said that as a church, nobody should be more loving and compassionate, and that we should be at the forefront of expressing love and outreach. The consistent counsel is: don't make love conditional on agreement.

## Answering the "normalizes sin" objection

- **Association is not approbation.** The Savior's ministry was, to His critics, a scandal of table fellowship — He ate with publicans and sinners and was condemned for it (Matt. 9:10–13; Luke 15:2). No Latter-day Saint reading of that ministry supports exclusion as a teaching tool.
- **Ostracism does not teach children doctrine; it teaches them that family love is contingent.** The lesson the cousins will actually absorb from an empty chair is that people can be disposed of. That is not the gospel.
- **Agency is the point.** The daughter has made a choice within her agency. Coercion — ultimatums, cold shoulders, relitigating at every meal — is the method of the adversary's plan, not the Father's. Contention drives away the Spirit (3 Ne. 11:29).
- **There is real risk on the other side.** Church leaders and Church-published resources have repeatedly acknowledged the harm — including suicide risk — that family rejection does to LGBTQ young people and adults. Rejection is not a neutral option.

## Practical navigation

1. **Keep the invitation standing and unconditional.** Sunday dinner is not an ordinance and requires no worthiness interview. The daughter, her wife, and the grandchildren come.
2. **Treat the wife by name and with courtesy.** Not "your friend," not invisible at the table. Ordinary hospitality costs nothing doctrinally and communicates everything relationally.
3. **Don't make the table a courtroom.** Say your position once, honestly, when asked; then stop. Repeated relitigation is what actually ends relationships. Silence about disagreement is not dishonesty — it's restraint.
4. **The grandchildren belong.** They can be blessed and baptized; they can certainly come to Thanksgiving.
5. **Let each set of parents teach their own children.** For younger cousins, the age-appropriate script is simple and true: "Our family believes God's plan for marriage is a husband and wife. Aunt ___ has chosen differently. We love her, and she is family." Children can hold both; adults often underestimate this.
6. **Boundaries, if any, should be about behavior and mutual respect — not about a person's presence.** Whether a couple shares a room in your home, how you describe the relationship to others, whether you attend a wedding — these are matters of individual and family judgment. The Church sets no policy on household social arrangements, and faithful families land in different places without any of them being in sin.
7. **Relatives who press for exclusion don't get a veto.** Their discomfort is not a doctrinal claim. A bishop can counsel, but no leader directs who sits at your table.

## The frame worth keeping

The two great commandments are not in tension here. Standing for the doctrine of eternal marriage and loving a daughter who has not embraced it are simultaneously possible — and the long game favors the family that stays connected. Doors that remain open can be walked through in either direction; doors slammed shut usually stay that way.

# Navigating Family Inclusion with a Same-Sex Married Daughter

This is one of the most personally consequential questions a Latter-day Saint family can face, and Church leaders have spoken to it with more directness than many members realize.

## What Senior Church Leaders Have Actually Said

**President Dallin H. Oaks** has addressed this scenario almost verbatim on multiple occasions:

> *"I can also imagine some circumstances in which it might be possible to say, 'Yes, come, but don't expect to stay overnight. Don't expect to be a filtered through anything other than what we've already taught in this home.'*"

More pointedly, he has taught that **parents should not cast out or sever ties** with children in same-sex relationships. In a 2006 interview and repeatedly since, he has drawn a clear line: maintaining a loving family relationship is not the same as endorsing every choice a family member makes.

**Elder Ballard** counseled: *"We need to listen to and understand what our LGBT brothers and sisters are feeling and experiencing. Certainly, we must do better than we have done in the past so that all members feel they have a spiritual home."*

## The Core Doctrinal Framework

A faithful Latter-day Saint can hold these truths simultaneously:

1. **The Proclamation on the Family** defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and the Church's doctrinal position on sexual morality has not changed.
2. **The second great commandment** — love thy neighbor — is not conditional on the neighbor's compliance with your understanding of the first.
3. **Agency is foundational to the Plan of Salvation.** Your daughter has exercised hers. Coercion through relational exile was literally the adversary's proposal.
4. **Christ ate with publicans and sinners** and was criticized for it by people who believed proximity was endorsement. He disagreed.

## Practical Guidance for the Family

**To the parents navigating this directly:**

- **Keep the Sunday dinner invitation open.** Your grandchildren's relationship with their grandparents, cousins, aunts, and uncles is not a theological concession — it is a family obligation. Children are never pawns in doctrinal disputes.
- **You don't need to performatively affirm or performatively object** at every gathering. Setting a place at the table is not a position paper. It's dinner.
- **Be honest when asked.** If your daughter asks what you believe, you can tell her — with kindness. If she doesn't ask, you don't need to volunteer a sermon. She already knows the Church's position. She grew up in your home.
- **Hold appropriate boundaries you'd hold for anyone.** The same household expectations about modesty, language, or media that apply to any guest apply here. No special rules are needed that single out her relationship.

**To the relatives who object:**

- **"Normalizing sin" is not a phrase found in scripture or General Conference.** The concern usually reflects a fear that younger family members will see the relationship and conclude the family approves. But children are far more confused by watching adults they love be excluded and shunned than by seeing a couple sit next to each other at Thanksgiving.
- **Your stewardship extends to your own children's teaching, not to policing the guest list.** If you are concerned about what your children understand, teach them at home — clearly, lovingly, and age-appropriately. That is your responsibility. Demanding that Grandma exile her daughter so you don't have to have a hard conversation is not faithfulness; it is avoidance.
- **Consider the fruits.** An ultimatum ("it's us or them at Christmas") forces a fracture that may never heal and drives people further from the Church, not closer. Ask whether that outcome serves anyone's salvation.

## What This Is Really About

The deepest doctrine in the Restoration is that **family bonds are meant to be eternal** — not disposable when they become complicated. A family that maintains love across profound disagreement models something more Christlike than a family that maintains unity through exclusion.

Your daughter is not asking you to change your beliefs. She is asking you to pass the potatoes. You can do both.

The Church does not recognize same-sex marriage as consistent with that standard. That doctrine isn't going to change to accommodate a family situation, and pretending otherwise isn't honest faithfulness.

- **Keep her at the table.** Welcoming your daughter, her wife, and the grandchildren to Sunday dinner and family gatherings is consistent with the gospel, not a betrayal of it. Inclusion is not endorsement; Christ ate with people whose lives didn't match His teachings, without ceasing to teach.

Kids can hold both; they do it constantly with other relatives whose choices differ from the family's standards (smoking, divorce, leaving the Church, etc.).
- *Exclusion teaches its own lesson.* What children actually absorb from shunning is that the family withdraws love when someone disappoints them—which is closer to the opposite of the gospel than the message the relatives intend.
- *Consistency matters.* Families rarely banish relatives for other departures from Church standards. Singling out this one tends to read as animus rather than principle, both to the daughter and to the kids.

**Boundaries are legitimate—on both sides.** Faithful inclusion doesn't mean the parents must stop expressing their beliefs, and it doesn't obligate the daughter to hide her marriage. The healthiest path is usually an explicit, kind conversation: the parents affirm their love and their desire for her to stay close, acknowledge their beliefs haven't changed, and ask what kind of relationship she wants. Mutual respect—she doesn't demand they renounce their faith; they don't make her presence conditional on hiding her family—lets the relationship endure.

**Bottom line:** A faithful Latter-day Saint family can hold firmly to the doctrine of marriage *and* keep a daughter, her wife, and grandchildren fully inside the circle of family love. ## Navigating This as a Faithful Latter-day Saint Family

This is one of the most genuinely difficult pastoral situations in contemporary LDS family life. There is no tension-free answer, but there is substantial church guidance, doctrinal principle, and lived wisdom to draw on.

---

### 1. What the Church Actually Teaches About Family Relationships

The Church's position on same-sex marriage is clear and unchanged: it is not recognized sacramentally, and participation in it affects a member's standing (temple recommend, callings). **But the Church's position on *family relationships* is equally clear and often underemphasized by members:**

- Elder Christofferson stated explicitly (2015 press conference): *"We want to be with our families… We love them. We're not going to reject them."*
- Elder Oaks (2019 General Conference and elsewhere) has consistently said that family members in same-sex marriages should be included in family life, not cut off.
- The General Handbook (38.6.23) addresses same-sex marriage in terms of *Church membership standing*, not in terms of instruction to sever family relationships.
- The Church's own resources (e.g., its *Gospel Topics* entry on same-sex attraction) explicitly counsel against rejection of family members.

**The "normalizing sin" argument, while sincerely felt, is not supported by church leadership's actual counsel.** No General Authority has taught that including a gay married child at Sunday dinner constitutes endorsement or "normalizes" sin to others.

---

### 2. Addressing the "Confusing the Cousins" Concern

This anxiety deserves a direct answer:

- **Children are not confused by love.** What confuses children is when adults around them model harshness toward family members and then teach them that the gospel is about love.
- Children in LDS families encounter the Church's teaching on marriage through Primary, family home evening, and personal study — not through observing who is invited to Thanksgiving.
- Parents of young cousins can and should teach their own children about LDS doctrine in their own homes. That is their stewardship. The solution to doctrinal questions is *teaching*, not exclusion.
- Ironically, research consistently shows that exclusion of gay family members is a significant driver of faith crises in LDS young adults who watch it happen. Witnessing a family choose harsh boundary-drawing over a sibling can shake testimony more than a gay aunt at Christmas.

---

### 3. The Distinction the Church Draws (and Families Must Learn)

The LDS framework distinguishes between:

| Level | Church's Position |
|---|---|
| **Doctrine** | Marriage is between man and woman; unchanged |
| **Church membership/ordinances** | Affected by participation in same-sex marriage |
| **Family relationship** | Should be maintained with love |
| **Personal endorsement** | Not required of family members |

You can be present at Sunday dinner without issuing a theological statement. Passing the rolls is not a press release.

---

### 4. What "Faithful Navigation" Actually Looks Like

**Do:**
- Welcome your daughter and her wife to family gatherings without conditions.
- Treat her wife with basic hospitality and dignity — this is fundamental to both the gospel and to human decency.
- Allow the grandchildren to have a relationship with their grandparents (this is enormously important to the children's wellbeing).
- Maintain honest, loving relationship with your daughter about your own faith and where you stand, without making every visit a referendum.
- Privately explain your own beliefs to younger relatives in age-appropriate ways if asked — that is your right as a parent/grandparent.

**Avoid:**
- Using family gatherings as occasions for doctrinal correction.
- Treating her wife differently than other in-laws (seating arrangements, introductions, photo inclusion, etc.).
- Letting relatives who advocate for exclusion set the terms of *your* family's relationship with *your* child.
- Conflating the Church's institutional policies with your personal family obligations.

---

### 5. On the Relatives Who Are Pressuring You

It is worth naming this plainly: **relatives who are pressuring you to exclude your daughter are not citing General Authority counsel — they are citing a folk-religion position that church leadership has not endorsed.** You are not obligated to conform your family relationships to their comfort.

You can respond:
> *"We've thought carefully about this, we love our daughter, and we're going to keep our relationship with her. We'd invite you to do the same, but that's between you and the Lord."*

---

### 6. The Harder Interior Work

Beyond the social navigation, faithful LDS parents in this situation commonly work through:

- **Grief** — for a temple sealing that won't happen, for the life they imagined
- **Theological wrestling** — what does "exaltation" mean for my child?
- **Integrity** — how do I hold my own beliefs without weaponizing them?

Many find it helpful to:
- Speak with a wise bishop who has pastoral (not just policy) experience
- Connect with other LDS parents in similar situations (e.g., the organization *PFLAG* has LDS members; the *North Star* community; some families find *Encircle* resources helpful)
- Pray specifically about *this child*, not about a category

---

### Bottom Line

The most defensible position from within LDS doctrine and from the counsel of Church leaders is this: **maintain the relationship, continue Sunday dinners, welcome the wife, love the grandchildren, and do not let the fear of what others will think sever a parent-child bond that the gospel itself places among the most sacred obligations a person has.**

The Savior's ministry was defined by who he ate with. That detail is not incidental.

# Ministering to him over the year

## First, get honest with myself
Before the first visit I have to settle a question: am I willing to minister to him for a year with no expectation that he ever comes back to church? If the answer is no, I should ask to be reassigned. He will smell an agenda within ten minutes, and he has every right to. What happened to his daughter — and what the bishop did with it — is a real injury, not a "concern" or a "stumbling block." If I show up framing it as anything less, I'm continuing the same institutional harm.

## The first visit
- Knock on the door as a neighbor, not as a representative. Introduce myself plainly: "I was assigned, you know that. I'd rather just be a friend if you'll let me. If you'd rather I not come back, tell me and I'll respect it."
- Don't bring a lesson, a *Liahona*, or a casserole-with-a-message. Bring nothing the first time, or bring something useful he didn't ask for a reason to refuse (a tool he can borrow, help with a yardwork project visible from the street).
- Name the elephant once, briefly: "I know what happened with your daughter and the bishop. I'm not here to defend anyone. I'm sorry it happened." Then drop it. Don't make him manage my feelings about it.
- Ask nothing about church. Ask about him — work, the kids, what he's into.
- Leave on time. Always leave on time.

## What I will *not* do
- I will not report on him to the elders quorum president or bishop beyond "I visited, he's well, please don't ask me for details." His life is not ward gossip.
- I will not bring up sacrament meeting, temple, tithing, the Word of Wisdom, or his record.
- I will not invite him to ward activities in the first six months unless he asks.
- I will not defend the bishop, the handbook, or the Church's abuse policies — even the improved ones. He doesn't need my apologetics; he needs witnesses to what was real.
- I will not pretend his daughter's experience is in the past. It isn't, for her or for him.

## The middle months
- Show up monthly, on a predictable cadence. Reliability is the entire sermon.
- Be useful: help him move a fridge, jump a car, watch his dog, bring soup when someone's sick — the unsexy stuff ministering was supposed to be before it became a metric.
- Ask about his daughter by name, gently, when it's natural. She is a person, not a wound. If she's open to it and he's comfortable, treat her with the dignity of a full human being — not as a "situation."
- If he wants to talk about what the bishop did, listen without flinching, without "yes, but," without redirecting to the Atonement. Believe him. Say so out loud: "That was wrong. They failed her and they failed you."
- Share my own life honestly. Tell him about my doubts, my frustrations with the institution, the things I don't have answers for. He has a finely tuned BS detector; the only currency that works is candor.

## When the church comes up
If *he* raises it — and only then — I can speak to my own relationship with God plainly, without proselytizing. I can distinguish between the gospel and the men. I can say: "I think you're right that men ran this badly. I haven't worked out what I do with that either. I keep coming because of [honest reason], but I'd understand if that doesn't move you." I will not promise that the church has fixed itself. I will tell him what I actually know about current abuse-reporting policy if he asks, and admit what's still inadequate.

## If he ever asks for something
- A priesthood blessing for his daughter or himself — give it, no strings, no follow-up "while I'm here let me also…"
- Help finding a therapist (especially one experienced with religious trauma and abuse) — quietly help, pay for a session if I can, never tell anyone.
- A bishop who will actually hear him — if he ever wants that, I'll go with him, advocate for him, and push back on leaders on his behalf. That's the real test of whether I'm his friend or the ward's informant.

## At a year
Success is not his return to activity. Success is: he picks up the phone when I call, his daughter is one step better supported than she was, he knows one Latter-day Saint who didn't lie to him or use him, and if he ever decides to walk back through the chapel doors it will be because he chose to — not because I wore him down.

And if a year in he's still where he started, I keep going. That's what the assignment actually is.

**First contact — name the assignment out loud.**

I don't arrive at his door with a message or a plate of cookies and a smile that pretends this is normal. I tell him the truth in the first two minutes: yes, I was assigned; yes, that's exactly the thing he said he distrusts; and no, I'm not going to pretend otherwise so I can get a foot in the door. Then I hand him control. He can tell me to leave, tell me once a year is plenty, tell me text-only, or tell me he'd rather I just be a neighbor and never mention the ward. I ask what he actually wants from me — and I let "nothing" be a real answer that I honor.

**Confidentiality, stated and then kept.**

He will assume, correctly, that I report to someone. So I say precisely what I will pass along: that contact happened, and nothing else. Not what he said about the bishop, not his family's business, not his standing. Then I go tell my elders quorum leaders that's the arrangement, and I hold it even when someone asks a well-meaning question in a Sunday meeting. If I break this once, the year is over. This is the concrete thing that either builds trust or doesn't.

**Believe him about the harm.**

His grievance is legitimate. A bishop mishandling an abuse disclosure is a real failure with real consequences for a real child, and I say that plainly — no "he was doing his best," no "you don't know the whole story," no pivot to the Church's improved policies as a rebuttal. If at some point he wants to know what the current expectations are — that bishops are required to call the abuse help line, that reporting obligations are taken far more seriously now — I can offer that as information he's entitled to, clearly framed as *this doesn't undo what happened to your daughter*. Information, not exoneration. And only if he asks.

I also take at face value his distinction between God and the men who run the church. I don't treat it as a cover story for a testimony problem or a sin problem. Scripturally I'm on solid ground agreeing with him: Section 121 exists precisely because men with authority abuse it, and the Lord's own assessment there is blunt. Nothing in my faith requires me to defend a bishop who failed a girl.

**Do not make his daughter a project.**

I don't ask for details of the abuse. I don't ask how she's doing as a way of getting information. I don't mention her to anyone in the ward, and I don't try to reach her around her father. If she ever wants help, that's hers to seek through channels she chooses. My assignment is him.

**The middle months — presence that isn't church-shaped.**

Ministering as it's actually taught has no required message, no required frequency, no attendance target, and nothing to count. So I don't count. I show up for things that matter to him and not to the ward: help with the truck, a standing invitation to breakfast, a text when his team loses, showing up at the funeral of someone he loved. If a hard week comes, I'm useful before I'm spiritual. Over months this either becomes a real friendship or it doesn't, and only one of those is my business to pursue.

If he ever wants to talk about the church, I follow rather than lead, and I don't flinch at anger. I don't defend the institution reflexively and I don't join in trashing it either — I can say honestly what I still believe while agreeing that what happened to his family was indefensible.

**If he wants recourse.**

At some point I'd mention, once, that the complaint has somewhere to go — the stake president, or higher — and that I'd sit beside him if he wanted to raise it. I promise no outcome. If he says no, I drop it permanently and never bring it up again as leverage.

**Month twelve.**

The likeliest honest outcome is that a year from now he is exactly where he is today: cordial, not attending, still angry, and correct to be. That is not a failed assignment. If he trusts one Latter-day Saint slightly more than he did — if he believes that at least one of us kept his confidence and didn't try to manage him back into a pew — then the ministry did what ministry is for. I'd ask to be kept on the assignment rather than rotated, because trust rebuilt at that pace can't survive a new stranger every March. And I'd tell him that: I'm not going anywhere, I'm not keeping score, and there's no version of this where I decide he's not worth the visit.

# Ministering to Someone Wounded by Institutional Betrayal

This is one of the most sacred and delicate assignments a ministering brother can receive. The man's grievance is **legitimate**—a bishop mishandled his daughter's abuse disclosure. His distrust isn't apostasy; it's a rational response to a real failure by someone who held ecclesiastical power over his family. That distinction must shape everything.

---

## Foundational Posture

**Before a single visit, internalize these truths:**

- He is right that the men failed him. You don't need to assess "how right." The Church's own policies now acknowledge that leaders sometimes mishandle abuse. You are not there to relitigate or defend what happened.
- He told you he doesn't have a problem with God. *Believe him.* That is an enormous statement of faith, not a half-measure. Many people in his position lose belief entirely.
- He sees you as an extension of the institution that hurt his daughter. Until proven otherwise, you *are* the ward's representative in his eyes, regardless of what you feel in your heart.
- His daughter is the primary victim. He is a secondary victim. Both realities matter.

---

## Months 1–3: Earn the Right to Be Present

**Goal: Become a person, not a program.**

- **First contact — be disarmingly honest.** Something like: *"I know the ward assigned me. I also know that probably doesn't mean much to you given what happened, and I understand why. I'm not here to get you back to church. I'd just like to know you."* Then follow his lead.
- **Don't bring church materials, messages from the bishop, or event invitations.** Nothing that signals "reactivation project." He will sniff that out instantly, and you'll lose him.
- **Find a shared interest and show up around that.** If he's working on his truck, show up with a socket set. If he watches football, text him during the game. If he gardens, bring him a tomato start in May. The medium doesn't matter; the message is *I see you as a human being, not a reclamation project.*
- **Never minimize, reframe, or spiritualize what happened.** If he brings it up, the correct responses are things like: *"That never should have happened to your daughter,"* or *"I'm sorry,"* or simply listening. Not *"leaders are imperfect"* or *"the Atonement can heal all wounds"*—both may be true, but spoken now they function as deflection.
- **Match his frequency.** If he wants monthly, do monthly. If he seems to welcome every-other-week, do that. Let him set the pace. Pressing in too fast confirms his suspicion that you have an agenda.

---

## Months 4–6: Demonstrate Trustworthiness Through Consistency

**Goal: Prove through repetition that you're not going away and you're not pivoting to reactivation.**

- **Keep showing up without escalating.** The most powerful thing you can do is be *boringly reliable.* Same guy, no agenda, keeps coming. Most ward members cycle through his life in a few months and disappear. Don't be that.
- **Protect his privacy fiercely.** When the elders quorum president asks how it's going, your answer is something like: *"He's a good man. We're building a friendship."* Full stop. Do not share details of his story, his feelings about the Church, or his daughter's situation. If he ever learns you reported back on him, it's over—and it should be.
- **If he tests you (and he will), pass the test.** He may say something provocative about the Church, about leaders, about the bishop specifically. He's watching to see if you flinch, get defensive, or start bearing testimony. The right response is usually to stay present and human: *"Yeah, I can see why you feel that way."*
- **Offer practical service without strings.** Help him move a couch, bring dinner when his wife is sick, remember his daughter's birthday. The theology of ministering is *"when ye are in the service of your fellow beings"*—and that needs no ecclesiastical wrapper.

---

## Months 7–9: Let Him Lead Any Spiritual Conversation

**Goal: Be available but never pushy if faith comes up.**

- By now, if you've been consistent and genuine, he may begin to open up more. He may share more about the original wound, about his daughter, about what he misses or doesn't miss.
- **If he expresses anything positive about faith or the gospel, gently affirm it without overreacting.** If he says, *"I do miss the hymns sometimes,"* don't immediately invite him to sacrament meeting. Just say, *"Which ones?"* and talk about music like two humans.
- **If he asks your opinion about something doctrinal or institutional, be honest.** He doesn't need a correlated answer—he needs to know you're a real person who wrestles with things too. Honesty about your own questions builds more trust than polished testimony.
- **If he never raises spiritual topics, that's completely fine.** You are not failing. A ministering brother who is a genuine, trusted friend to a wounded man *is the ministry.* There is no next step that needs to happen.

---

## Months 10–12: Sustain the Relationship Regardless of "Outcomes"

**Goal: Make clear this isn't a year-long project with a deadline.**

- **Don't do a year-end assessment in your head.** If you find yourself thinking *"it's been a year and he still hasn't come back,"* you have revealed your actual agenda to yourself. Repent of that framing. He is not a metric.
- **Ask how his daughter is doing** (if appropriate and if he's opened that door). Her healing matters. If she hasn't received proper support—therapy, justice, ecclesiastical acknowledgment—that wound is still open and his absence makes complete sense.
- **If the institutional failure was never formally acknowledged, consider whether you have standing to advocate.** This is delicate, but if the current bishop is a good man and the original bishop's mishandling was never addressed, there may be a time to privately tell your bishop: *"This family was failed, and no one has ever said so."* Whether and how to do this depends entirely on the man's wishes. **Never advocate without his knowledge and consent.**
- **Continue into year two with the same posture.** If reassignments happen, advocate to keep him. Continuity is everything with betrayal trauma.

---

## What You Report to the Elders Quorum

Keep it brief and protective:
- *"We're building a friendship. He's a good man. He has real reasons for his distance, and I'm respecting his pace."*
- If pressed for details: *"I don't think it's my place to share his story. I'd rather keep his trust."*
- If pressured for "progress": *"I think being a consistent, safe presence is the most important thing I can do right now."*

---

## The Hard Truth

There is a real possibility that after a year of faithful ministering, he will not return to church. **That is not a failure.** The failure already happened—years ago, in a bishop's office, when his daughter needed protection and received something less.

Your calling is not to undo that. Your calling is to be evidence—small, consistent, lived evidence—that the body of Christ includes people who will show up, shut up, and love without conditions. If he ever does come back, it will be because someone proved the institution could produce a man worth trusting.

Be that man. And if he never comes back, be that man anyway.

## Ministering to a Man Wounded by Institutional Betrayal

### The Foundational Assessment

Before anything else: **his grievance is legitimate.** A bishop mishandled his daughter's abuse disclosure. That is a real failure with real victims, not a misunderstanding or a faith crisis born of offense. Any approach that treats his absence as a spiritual problem to solve rather than a wound to acknowledge will fail and confirm his suspicion that the ward sent a fixer, not a friend.

His own words are the key: *"I don't have a problem with God."* That is not apostasy — that is a man who separated the institution from the divine because the institution failed him catastrophically. He has done precise theological work. Honor it.

---

### Year-Long Framework

#### Months 1–3: Earn the Right to Be There

**Show up without an agenda visible to him.** Early visits should be brief, low-pressure, and focused entirely on him as a man — his work, his interests, his family, his life now. Ask questions. Listen without redirecting to church topics.

**Acknowledge the wound early and plainly.** Not defensively, not with institutional hedging. Something like: *"I know you left for serious reasons. I'm not here to pretend that didn't happen or to argue you back."* This is disarming because it's the opposite of what he expects.

**Do not report back to the bishop in any way that resembles surveillance.** If he ever senses you are gathering intelligence about him for the ward, the relationship is over. Your ministerial report should say "we visited and had good conversation" — nothing more without his consent. This is a real tension with ward culture; resolve it in his favor.

**Practical service over symbolic visits.** If he needs help with something — yard work, a move, a repair — show up in jeans, not in a white shirt carrying a pass-along card. Labor alongside him. This is the oldest form of human trust-building.

**Do not defend the institution in months 1–3.** You have not yet earned the standing to have that conversation, and attempting it will read as loyalty to the system over loyalty to him.

---

#### Months 3–6: Deepen Presence, Expand Trust

By now you have some relational texture. He knows you keep coming. He likely wonders why. When he tests you — and he will — answer honestly:

*"Because I actually like you. And I think what happened to your family was wrong. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."*

This is the moment many ministering brothers fail. They revert to program language when tested. Stay human.

**Let him vent about the church without flinching.** He needs to know that candor won't make you disappear or become defensive. When he describes the bishop's mishandling, say: *"That should never have happened. There's no version of that where he handled it right."* Validation is not disloyalty to the church — it is truthfulness, and it is what he has been denied.

**Find common ground in what he still believes.** He believes in God. He may still hold doctrinal convictions. Conversations about faith, meaning, scripture, or Christ can happen entirely outside the frame of "the church." Follow his lead. If he goes there, go with him. If he doesn't, don't force it.

**Introduce your own humanity.** Share your own doubts, your own frustrations with institutional failures, your own wrestling. You are not an ambassador of a perfect church. You are a flawed person who has chosen to stay — and being honest about the costs of that choice makes you credible.

---

#### Months 6–9: The Honest Conversation About Institutions

If the relationship has grown, he will eventually ask you something like: *"How do you stay after what they do to people?"* This is not an attack — it is an invitation to real dialogue. Engage it fully.

**Acknowledge the structural problem.** Local leaders have enormous discretionary power, minimal training in trauma and abuse, and a cultural pressure to handle things internally. These are facts. Saying them is not apostasy.

**Distinguish between the covenant/doctrine and the administration.** This is a distinction he has already made — reinforce it. The Restoration's truth claims, the covenants, the theology of eternal families — these do not rise or fall on whether a bishop in a specific ward made a correct decision in a specific crisis.

**Never minimize what happened to his daughter.** If the conversation ever gets abstract enough that it feels like the institutional question is being weighed against a real child's harm, return to the concrete: *"Whatever else we disagree about, what happened to her was wrong, and it should have been handled differently."* Full stop, every time.

**Surface the possibility of distinguishing between returning to God and returning to the ward.** Not as a pitch. As an honest observation: *"You never lost your relationship with God. That might matter more than what you do with the ward."*

---

#### Months 9–12: Long-term Presence, Low Expectations

**Do not measure success by sacrament meeting attendance.** A man who was spiritually abused by an institution returning to that institution is a long, nonlinear process — if it happens at all, and it may not. Success at one year looks like: he trusts you as a genuine friend, he knows someone in the church sees his pain clearly, and he has not closed the door on God.

**Consider whether any formal acknowledgment or accountability would be healing.** In some cases, a current bishop reaching out specifically to acknowledge what happened — not to recruit him back, but to say *"what was done to your family was wrong and I'm sorry"* — can be meaningful. This is worth exploring carefully, only if the current bishop is actually capable of that conversation without making it about retention.

**Continue showing up.** The most powerful thing you will have done by December is simply kept coming — not as an emissary, but as a person who chose him. That is, in fact, the gospel he lost faith in, embodied without announcing itself.

---

### What Not to Do

- **Don't bear your testimony unprompted** in early visits. It reads as recruitment.
- **Don't suggest his pain is a faith trial to overcome.** It is a wound caused by real people making real wrong decisions.
- **Don't say "the church is perfect, people aren't."** He knows this. It has been used to dismiss his daughter's harm. It will end the relationship.
- **Don't set internal benchmarks** ("if he's not back by Easter, I failed"). These will distort your motives and he will sense it.
- **Don't tell the ward council details** of what he shares with you in trust.

---

### The Underlying Principle

He left because men who claimed authority from God used it to harm his daughter and then protected themselves. The only thing that can reach him is a man who claims that same connection but uses it to protect *him* — his dignity, his pain, his trust — with no institutional benefit to himself. That is a years-long project. Begin it without any expectation of completion within a year. Begin it because it is right.

This is one of the hardest ministering situations—and one where conventional "fellowship him back" approaches will backfire. Here's how I'd approach the year:

## First: Accept the Legitimacy of His Position

His daughter's abuse disclosure was mishandled by a bishop. That's not "being offended"—that's institutional failure at a moment of profound vulnerability. His distrust isn't a spiritual problem to solve. It's a reasonable response to real harm.

His theological distinction ("I don't have a problem with God") is actually sophisticated. Honor it.

## The First Few Months: Deprogram Yourself

**Stop thinking of yourself as "sent."** He's right to distrust that framing. You're not an agent of the institution—you're a neighbor who happens to share geography and (complicated) religious heritage.

- Don't report personal details to elders quorum presidency. "We talked. He's doing fine" is enough.
- Don't invite him to church. Don't bring up church at all unless he does.
- Find genuine points of connection—hobbies, work, neighborhood stuff.
- Be consistent. Show up. He's learned church people disappear when you're not useful.

## When He Tests You (He Will)

At some point he'll likely say something critical of the Church or leadership to see how you react. 

**Don't defend. Don't explain. Don't "both sides" it.**

"What happened to your daughter—and to your family—shouldn't have happened. I'm sorry it did."

That's it. Witness the wound. Don't try to heal it with words.

## If Trust Develops

Let him lead any spiritual conversations. If he talks about what happened:
- Listen completely
- Don't minimize ("leaders are imperfect but called of God")
- Don't weaponize forgiveness ("have you considered forgiving the bishop?")
- Don't make it about his return ("the Church needs people like you")

He may share that he still prays, reads scripture, or feels close to God. Affirm that. His faith outside institutional walls is real.

## What Success Looks Like

Here's the hard part: by institutional metrics, you may "fail." He may never come back to church. That doesn't mean you failed him.

Success is:
- He knows one person from the ward who showed up without agenda
- His experience of "church people" includes someone who didn't defend the indefensible
- If his family ever needs help, he'd feel comfortable calling you

## The Deeper Principle

You're not ministering *to get him back*. You're ministering because he's a child of God who was hurt, and presence without agenda is what Christlike love looks like when institutions have failed.

Some people return. Some don't. Your job is to love him either way—and to be honest with yourself about whether you can do that without attachment to outcomes.

# Ministering to a Less-Active Member with Institutional Distrust

**Build trust through consistent presence, not assignment.**

- **Don't lead with the calling.** Visit as yourself, not "your ministering brother." Acknowledge the awkwardness: "I know you didn't ask for this, and I'm not here to argue you back to church."

- **Listen more than you teach.** His grievance is legitimate. Let him describe what happened and what it cost him. Don't defend the bishop or institution—that confirms his distrust. Validate: "That was a failure. Your daughter deserved better protection."

- **Demonstrate institutional accountability exists somewhere.** He may benefit knowing about channels he didn't know about then (Title IX offices, survivor advocacy resources, ecclesiastical review processes). This isn't excusing the past—it's showing the institution can be held to standards.

- **Separate your credibility from the ward's.** Over months, let him see you as a person with integrity, not a representative. Ask his advice. Admit uncertainty. Be vulnerable about your own questions about the church's culture. Don't pretend the problem doesn't exist.

- **Respect the boundary he set.** He's already told you what he needs: genuine relationship, not institutional recovery. If he never comes back to Sunday meetings, that's not your failure. His faith in God might be real and private. Ministry might mean being the friend who shows up, not the asset who converts.

- **Address the structural problem he's naming.** Over the year, support actual reforms: abuse disclosure training, survivor support, transparency. Show the church can change. Don't ask him to forgive before the institution repents.

**The goal isn't conversion—it's proving some men in the church take his daughter's experience seriously.**

The approach should be characterized by deep patience, unconditional acceptance, and an absolute commitment to focusing ministry entirely on the individual rather than attempting to immediately repair institutional or relational structures.

Here is a framework for ministering to him over the coming year:

### Phase 1: Establish Unconditional Listening (Months 1-3)
The primary goal during this phase is not evangelism or doctrinal teaching, but establishing authentic trust by proving that your presence does not carry the agenda of "the ward."

*   **Listen More Than You Speak:** Dedicate time in every interaction to simply hearing his perspective without formulating an immediate defense or offering solutions. Validate his anger and his perception of betrayal as genuine experiences. Phrases like, "It sounds like what you went through was profoundly painful and deeply felt," are vital.
*   **Respect His Boundaries on Authority:** Acknowledge his distrust explicitly, but do not challenge it directly. Instead, respect his autonomy. If he states that he doesn't trust the leaders sent by the ward, accept that as his reality for now. Focus your ministry solely on what you can offer him personally and ethically within your role—your integrity, compassion, and consistent presence.
*   **Focus on Shared Humanity:** Shift conversations away from institutional politics or theology, and toward shared human experiences—grief, loss, the search for safety, enduring hardship. This builds connection based on mutual experience rather than imposed belief systems.

### Phase 2: Consistent Presence and Service (Months 4-8)
Once a baseline of respectful listening is established, ministry shifts into sustained service that demonstrates reliability over time.

*   **Be Reliable:** Show up consistently. If you commit to checking in weekly, do it without demanding immediate progress or emotional reciprocity from him. Reliability builds the foundational trust necessary for anyone to consider opening up again.
*   **Focus on Personal Well-being:** Since he is less active, focus ministry on his personal health, quiet moments of reflection, and finding small areas where he feels agency over his life—activities that are entirely within his control. This allows him to reclaim a sense of self outside the context of institutional failure.
*   **Offer Resources, Not Demands:** If appropriate, connect him with non-judgmental resources (counseling referrals, quiet study materials, or community connections) without pressuring him into using them. The goal is to offer support passively until he signals readiness for active engagement.

### Phase 3: Dialogue on Hope and Identity (Months 9-12+)
As the year progresses, you can begin gently exploring themes of hope and identity, always keeping the focus on his internal journey, not the external structure.

*   **The Personal vs. The System:** If the opportunity arises to discuss faith or community, frame it entirely around how he defines a meaningful life or purpose for himself, rather than debating church doctrine or bishop conduct. You might say: "What kind of support helps you feel grounded when things are difficult?"
*   **Patience with Change:** Understand that his distrust is rooted in specific past events. Healing from such wounds takes years. Your role is not to accelerate this timeline; it is to be a steady, safe harbor where he can exist without the pressure to trust the entire structure immediately.
*   **Maintain Non-Judgmental Distance:** Continue to minister with profound humility and self-awareness. If you become defensive about his past or tempted to "fix" him, you risk triggering another sense of institutional alienation. Maintain a posture of loving presence—a steady light available, but never demanding he walk toward it.

In summary: The strategy is **slow immersion**. Ministering to him means becoming a source of trustworthy humanity that exists outside the system he distrusted, proving through consistent action and unwavering respect that true spiritual support can be found in individual relationships rather than institutional mandates.

I ask about who he is, not just about the fact. Is there someone he likes? Who at school knows? What's it been like at church?

I make it explicit that getting help is normal and not a punishment. I find him a therapist who is competent with LGBTQ youth and who will not attempt to change his orientation. I ask him directly, more than once, whether he's had thoughts of hurting himself.

# In This Moment

You hold him. Before a single word of theology or policy, you hold your son and let him feel in his body what you are about to say with your mouth:

**"I love you. I am not going anywhere, and neither are you. This is your home."**

Then you answer his two questions directly, because he asked directly and he deserves clarity, not deflection:

**"Do I still want you here?"** *Yes. There is nothing you could tell me that would make me not want you here. You are my son. That is not conditional.*

**"Does God still want you?"** *Yes. And that is not my opinion — it is doctrine.* Every person is a child of Heavenly Parents, possessed of eternal worth and divine nature that is not diminished, altered, or made conditional by the experience of same-sex attraction. You can point him, when the moment is calm enough, to the Church's own language: "The experience of same-sex attraction is a complex reality for many people. The attraction itself is not a sin" (*General Handbook* 38.6.16; see also the Church's official resource at ChurchofJesusChrist.org on same-sex attraction). God does not stop wanting someone He made.

You do not try to explain everything tonight. Tonight is about safety, attachment, and trust.

---

# In the Days and Weeks That Follow

## 1. Secure the Relationship First

Adolescents who come out to rejecting families face dramatically elevated risks of depression, self-harm, substance abuse, and suicide. Research (e.g., the Family Acceptance Project, San Francisco State University) consistently shows that **family acceptance is the single strongest protective factor** — even within a framework that holds to the Church's law of chastity. You can hold a doctrinal line about sexual conduct without communicating rejection of your child as a person. These are not the same thing, and conflating them is dangerous.

Practical steps:
- Tell him explicitly and repeatedly that your love is not contingent on this.
- Do not treat his disclosure as a crisis, a phase, or a problem to be solved.
- Ask him what he needs. Listen more than you teach.
- Watch for signs of depression or self-harm and secure professional support (a therapist experienced with LGBTQ+ youth *and* respectful of faith) if needed.

## 2. Distinguish Between Attraction and Conduct — Carefully and Humbly

The Church's current position distinguishes between experiencing same-sex attraction (not sinful) and acting on it sexually (considered a violation of the law of chastity, which applies to heterosexual members outside of marriage as well). You can teach this framework honestly:

- He has not sinned by being gay. He has not sinned by telling you.
- The law of chastity as currently taught by the Church asks all unmarried members — regardless of orientation — to abstain from sexual relations.
- You acknowledge openly that this standard asks something profoundly harder of him than of his heterosexual peers, because current Church policy does not provide a path to a sanctioned same-sex marriage. You do not minimize that cost. You name it.

## 3. Preserve His Place in the Church — If He Wants It

He said he already feels like he doesn't belong. That feeling is real, and it likely comes from things he has heard at church — jokes, casual comments, cultural attitudes that go well beyond official doctrine. You become his advocate:

- Talk with his bishop, if your son is willing, to ensure he has priesthood leaders who will treat him with the sensitivity the Church's own handbook requires.
- Challenge homophobic comments in Sunday School, quorum meetings, and family gatherings — not performatively, but consistently. He needs to see you do this.
- Remind him that he is eligible for full participation: temple attendance, priesthood service, callings, mission — all of these are open to him.
- If a specific ward environment is genuinely toxic, you consider whether a different ward might offer safer ground. The Church is true in every building; not every building is equally safe.

## 4. Hold Space for Uncertainty — Including Your Own

You will likely grieve. Not because something is wrong with your son, but because the future you imagined for him — temple marriage, a family that mirrors your own — may look different than you expected. That grief is human. Process it with your spouse, with a counselor, with God. **Do not process it with your son.** He cannot carry your grief on top of his own fear.

You also hold space for doctrinal humility. The Church's understanding of homosexuality has evolved significantly even within the past two decades (compare the rhetoric of the 1970s–90s with current official statements). You can be faithful to current prophetic teaching while acknowledging that "we believe that He will yet reveal many great and important things pertaining to the Kingdom of God" (Article of Faith 9). You do not promise him that the policy will change. You do not promise him it won't. You teach him that faithfulness and uncertainty can coexist — that is, in fact, the definition of faith.

## 5. Let Him Set the Pace

He may want to stay fully active. He may need a break. He may cycle between the two. Your job is to make clear that his standing in your family is not indexed to his church attendance. You walk beside him. You do not drag him, and you do not abandon him.

---

# The Doctrinal Heart of It

The two great commandments are to love God and to love your neighbor — and Christ specified that the second is *like unto* the first. Your son is not just your neighbor; he is your stewardship, your covenant child. The parable of the lost sheep is not about a sheep that did something wrong — it is about a shepherd who noticed one was missing and considered that intolerable.

Your son told you he is afraid. The single most Christlike thing you can do is make sure he never has to be afraid of that again — not in your home.

## In the Moment

**What you say first matters most.** Your son has carried this alone, in terror of losing you. The doctrine can wait. The person in front of you cannot.

## On "Does God still want me?"

This is the question underneath the question, and it deserves a careful, honest, LDS-grounded answer — not a deflection.

**What you can say with full doctrinal confidence:**

> *"Yes. Absolutely yes. You are a beloved child of Heavenly Father. That is not conditional on who you're attracted to. The Church teaches clearly that experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin — it is not a moral failing, not a sign God has rejected you, not a flaw in your spirit. You are not broken.
